questions.q: With the starting Mars plan, how much propellant must be in the ship's tanks before it leaves Earth orbit, and how many tanker flights fill it?
questions.do: Keep Destination: Mars and the starting settings. Read the Propellant table and the summary line above Fly this plan.
questions.a: 564 t are needed in the tanks, and it takes 6 tanker flights over 42 days.

questions.q: How does the size of each tanker change the number of tanker flights?
questions.do: Move Propellant per tanker to 150 t and read the summary line. Then move it to 50 t.
questions.a: At 150 t per tanker it takes 4 flights (28 days). At 50 t it takes 11 flights (77 days). Smaller loads mean more trips to deliver the same propellant.

questions.q: What does it cost to get to Mars in the shortest trip time?
questions.do: Drag Trip time all the way to the fastest setting (112 days) and read the Velocity budget and Propellant tables.
questions.a: The Mars entry speed becomes 12.02 km/s, above the 7.5 km/s heat-shield limit, so a 4.52 km/s braking burn is added. The tanks now need about 4,262 t, against 564 t for the 259-day trip.

questions.q: Why does a Moon landing need a bigger velocity budget than a Mars landing?
questions.do: Read the Total from Earth orbit in the Velocity budget for Mars. Then click Moon and read the total again.
questions.a: Mars needs 4.34 km/s from Earth orbit; the Moon needs 8.90 km/s. The Moon has no air to brake on, so every slowdown must be a rocket burn. At Mars the atmosphere does most of the braking, leaving only a 0.75 km/s landing burn.

questions.q: How close were the old Indian astronomy texts to modern values for the length of the year and of Mars's year?
questions.do: Scroll to Ancient Indian astronomy still finds this month's Mars window and read the rows Sidereal year and Mars year in the table.
questions.a: The Surya Siddhanta gives a sidereal year of 365.25876 days and the Aryabhatiya (499 CE) 365.25868; the modern value is 365.25637. All four ancient texts give Mars's year as 687.00 days; the modern value is 686.98. Very close, after more than a thousand years.
